mcqs.q: A Class II preparation is located on the:
mcqs.explain: Preparations on the proximal surfaces of posterior teeth are Class II.

mcqs.q: The two Class II composite preparation designs are:
mcqs.explain: A Class II composite preparation may be conventional or modified in design.

mcqs.q: The MODIFIED Class II design is characterised by:
opts: Smaller burs; more rounded, less boxlike, less uniform preparation
mcqs.explain: The modified design (for smaller restorations) uses smaller burs and is more rounded, less boxlike and less uniform in depth/extension.

mcqs.q: The conventional Class II preparation has two components:
opts: The occlusal step and the proximal box
The pulp chamber and root canal
mcqs.explain: The conventional Class II has an occlusal step portion and a proximal box portion.

mcqs.q: The occlusal step of a Class II preparation is prepared similarly to:
mcqs.explain: The occlusal portion of the Class II is prepared much like a Class I preparation.

mcqs.q: Which bur is used to enter (punch cut) the occlusal step?
mcqs.explain: The pit nearest the proximal surface is entered with a punch cut using a No. 245 bur (or the smaller, pear-shaped No. 330).

mcqs.q: The No. 330 bur, compared with the No. 245, is:
mcqs.explain: The No. 330 bur is a smaller, pear-shaped version of the No. 245 bur.

mcqs.q: When cutting, the bur should be:
opts: Rotating before it contacts the tooth and until it is removed, parallel to the long axis
Stopped, then started in the tooth
mcqs.explain: The bur must already be rotating on contact and keep rotating until removed; it is held parallel to the long axis of the tooth.

mcqs.q: The pulpal floor is prepared to a depth of about:
mcqs.explain: The pulpal floor is prepared to ~1.5 mm depth, measured from the central groove, and is relatively flat.

mcqs.q: The dovetail in the opposite (distal) pit functions to:
opts: Resist mesial displacement of the restoration
mcqs.explain: The distal-pit dovetail provides retention form that may prevent mesial displacement of the completed restoration.

mcqs.q: A dovetail outline in the distal pit is NOT required if:
mcqs.explain: A dovetail in the distal pit is unnecessary when there are no radiating fissures to include.

mcqs.q: The isthmus width should preferably be no wider than:
opts: One quarter of the intercuspal distance
Three quarters of the intercuspal distance
mcqs.explain: The isthmus should be as narrow as possible, ideally ≤ ¼ of the intercuspal distance.

mcqs.q: Ideally the occlusal step width equals that of the:
mcqs.explain: Ideally the preparation is the width of the No. 245 bur (~0.8 mm); narrow restorations give longer clinical service.

mcqs.q: Which is MORE important to restoration longevity?
opts: The amount of remaining tooth structure
mcqs.explain: Generally the amount of remaining tooth structure matters more to longevity than the restorative material used.

mcqs.q: When extending mesially (for an MO), the preparation should stop approximately:
opts: 0.8 mm short of the marginal ridge
mcqs.explain: Maintaining pulpal depth, the preparation is extended mesially to stop ~0.8 mm short of the marginal ridge before the box is cut.

mcqs.q: In the box region, the occlusal portion is made:
opts: Slightly wider faciolingually than in a Class I (to receive the box)
mcqs.explain: The occlusal portion near the box is made slightly wider faciolingually because additional width is needed for the proximal box.

mcqs.q: The proximal box of a Class II preparation:
opts: Breaks the proximal contact and has gingival/axial/facial/lingual walls
mcqs.explain: The proximal box breaks contact and is bounded by gingival, axial, facial and lingual walls.

mcqs.q: If only one proximal surface is restored, you should:
opts: Maintain the opposite marginal-ridge dentinal support
mcqs.explain: When restoring only one proximal surface, the opposite marginal-ridge dentinal support should be preserved.

mcqs.q: Before placing a Class II composite, a matrix band and wedge are used to:
opts: Rebuild contour/contact and prevent gingival overhang
mcqs.explain: A contoured matrix and wedge re-establish proximal contour and contact and prevent a gingival overhang.

mcqs.q: Narrow Class II restorations are preferred because they:
opts: Provide a greater length of clinical service
mcqs.explain: Narrow restorations preserve tooth structure and give a greater length of clinical service.

mcqs.q: Air-water spray during high-speed cutting is used to:
opts: Cool the tooth and bur and clear debris
mcqs.explain: High-speed cutting uses air-water spray to cool the tooth/bur and wash away debris, preventing thermal pulp damage.

mcqs.q: The proximal box is cut to break contact with the:
opts: Marginal ridge of the same tooth
mcqs.explain: The proximal box is extended faciolingually and gingivally to clear (break) contact with the adjacent tooth.

saqs.q: Define a Class II preparation and name its two conventional components.
saqs.a: Preparation on the proximal surface of a posterior tooth; components = occlusal step + proximal box.

saqs.q: Which burs enter the occlusal step, and how is the bur held?
saqs.a: No. 245 (or smaller pear-shaped No. 330); held parallel to the long axis, rotating before contact.

saqs.q: Give the pulpal-floor depth and the ideal isthmus width.
saqs.a: Pulpal floor ~1.5 mm from the central groove; isthmus ≤ ¼ of the intercuspal distance (≈ 0.8 mm).

saqs.q: What is the purpose of the distal-pit dovetail, and when is it omitted?
saqs.a: Resists mesial displacement of the restoration; omitted if there are no radiating fissures.

saqs.q: Where does the mesial extension stop, and why is the occlusal made wider there?
saqs.a: Stops ~0.8 mm short of the marginal ridge; made wider faciolingually to receive the proximal box.
It breaks the proximal contact and has gingival, axial, facial and lingual walls.

saqs.q: What matters most to longevity, and why use a matrix/wedge?
saqs.a: Remaining tooth structure matters most; matrix + wedge rebuild contour/contact and prevent overhang.
